utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours; good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. Today is Monday. I would like to firstly greet the witness. I would like to greet the accused, the Defence counsel, the members of the OTP, as well as all the people assisting us. I shall first of all give the floor to the registrar who has an IC number to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Petkovic Defence has submitted its response to the Prosecution's objections to documents tendered through expert witness Josip Jurcevic. This list shall be given Exhibit IC1051. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I would like to read out an oral decision. Proprio motu oral decision on the filing of the Praljak Defence motion pursuant to guideline 9 of the Trial Chamber's decision on the 24th of April, 2008. The Trial Chamber recalls its decision in which it adopted the guidelines on the presentation of the Defence case handed down on the 24th of April, 2008, in particular paragraph 35 on guideline 9 which states that any motion on the admission of documentary evidence must be filed as soon as possible after the presentation of all evidence on a given municipality or a specific topic. The Trial Chamber notices that to date the Praljak Defence has not filed a written motion on the admission of evidence pursuant to guideline 9, and the Trial Chamber knows nothing about what it intends to do in that regard. The Trial Chamber recalls that the Defence teams must not wait for the end of their case to file such motions. The Trial Chamber therefore requests the Praljak Defence team to kindly let the Trial Chamber know before midday on the 1st of October, 2009, what it intends to do as regards the filing of one or several motions pursuant to guideline 9, and if it intends to do so, on what topics and in what time-frame will it file such requests. In other words, the Trial Chamber is asking the Praljak Defence team to let it know whether it has any intention of filing such motions with a view to having documentary evidence admitted. We would like this to be done, therefore, before the 1st of October, 2009. The deadline is midday. Mr. Kovacic, you have understood me well, have you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for that reminder. It is my honour to inform you that about an hour ago we did file a notice where -- with the general information. It still hasn't been received, but I do see that it was sent out to the Registry, so in an hour or half an hour it will be received, and then we can inform the Trial Chamber about some additional matters, but we took advantage of the opportunity you gave us a few days ago to provide plans for Witness 3DA, and then we also informed you with respect to guideline number 9, but you'll see all that in the course of the day and if necessary we'll add on to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second point: You have also told us on the 28th of September, i.e., today, that Witness 3DA is not going to be coming, which means that your last witness, according to the schedule you have given us, will be coming on Tuesday, the 13th of October. After that, we will have no witness on the 14th, 15th of October, and then in the following week, and we shall resume on the 26th of October, and we will then be hearing the witness of the Petkovic Defence team. Mr. Kovacic, is that what has been scheduled or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely, Your Honour. And I've just remembered that we sent your assistants a courtesy copy, but obviously you already have it in your hands. But in the last paragraph we just, in brief, set out what our intentions are with respect to the motion for documentary evidence in conformity with guideline number 9. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will therefore resume on the 26th of October. We have a problem, however, with our schedule. This would be at quarter past 2.00 on the Monday, but on the 26th of October this is the date when the elections for the President of this Tribunal are being conducted, and this starts at 2.00 in the afternoon. This may be quick or it may not. It depends how many candidates there are, one, two, or three. Much will depend on that. Therefore, we have every reason to believe that we will start our hearing on the 26th of October at 4.00 most probably. At 4.00 p.m., normally speaking, the elections should be over. So please pencil this in so that we can make our arrangements. Initially, as I am a permanent Judge and since I need to vote, I felt that there was no point in going, but since my colleagues would like to attend, we will therefore start at 4.00 p.m. There will be a slight gap, but we can't work it out any other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I simply would like to say that there was a mistake when you mentioned that we should only finish on that very day of 26th of October. It is written here that at 4.00, normally speaking, the elections should be over, but the -- what I believe you also added that we would then finish our sitting at 1800 hours, meaning at 6.00 p.m. So 6.00 p.m. should be inserted here, because then it is when -- if I understood correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. On the transcript in English, 1800 hours was never mentioned, 6.00 was never mentioned, and I never talked about 6.00 p.m. Let me remind you that the elections for the president of this Tribunal start at 2.00 p.m. This should take two hours. This means that we will finish that at 4.00. We will therefore be able to start hearing the expert witness on 4.00 that afternoon. Everything's clear. Ms. Alaburic still had questions, since you have the lectern. According to our timing, you should have 15 minutes left and no more, but before I give you the floor, let me address the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Witness, thanks to these few days we have had between your testimony last week and today, I was able to reflect on a number of matters, and I have two technical questions to put to you. With hindsight one is able to realise sometimes that it is important to clarify a number of points. In French, on several occasions, you used the expression "military region." In your language, we had the expression "operational zone" and not "military region." When in French you say "military region," are we to understand that this means the same thing as operational zone, or is this something different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This means operational zone. A military region or district, as far as I'm concerned, would be Tomislavgrad for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it means one and the same thing. On looking at a number of documents, I realised that in some of the orders operational zones were mentioned, OZ for short. And sometimes the word "military district" was used, ZP for short. OZ and ZP, does it mean the same thing? Is it the same thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember exactly what ZP means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This should mean military district.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Zborno podrucje," I believe this means military region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So basically it's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second question of a technical nature. As far as the military police is concerned, last week you told us that there was the real military police and then there was also the military police incorporated in the brigade. Does it mean this: Does it mean that there is a military police which comes under the authority of the military police administration in a chain of command, and that would be the real military police, and then there are also military policemen inside the brigades who, as you have told us, are soldiers who are called military police soldiers inside the brigades; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is quite right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question now, also of a technical nature, General. Did you know that during the fighting some units of the real military police, the military police that was a part of the chain of command and not included in the brigades, had sometimes been subordinated to brigades and that these took part in some of the fighting? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The real military police was never subordinated to the brigades, but these men did take part in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you are telling us is important, General, because General Praljak told us the opposite. Let me explain this to you. General Praljak told us as follows: For combat operations a brigade commander or an operational zone brigade may ask the military police administration to subordinate some of their men who are then placed under the authority and the sole authority of the brigade commander. This is what he has told us, and now you have just told me the opposite. Could you clarify this for us, and why is there a difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that when the military police was brought to a combat area, they then reported to the command of a military region and reported directly to the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are saying that they then reported to two commands. Do you mean from an operational standpoint, or do you mean from its authority if an investigation needed to be conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From an operational standpoint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you have just told us is now on the transcript, but so far we have understood the opposite. I understood. Perhaps the other members of the Bench may like to say something on this subject. What I understood is this: When a unit of the military police is sent to a unit, let's say X, and is to conduct military operations. It's then the commander of the brigade who is exercising full command over his men, and yet he tells them then that you are going to take up such-and-such a position, you're going to do this and that, and these military policemen have only one commander. That is the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander of a brigade gave the orders on the ground, but let me repeat, despite that the military police also took its orders from the head of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it is -- this is possible. We need to clarify this. If there are two commanders who can give orders that both are entitled to do this, this will be rather disorderly. Could you not clarify this for us, please? In administrative terms, the military policemen were still part of the police administration, whereas as far as their work on the ground while they are part of the brigade, it is only the brigade commander who tells them what they must do on the battle-field.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this has made things clear, and we have been able to iron out some of these differences we had. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answers. These questions were, in my mind, important ones. Last question which has to do with your credibility and personality. At the beginning of last week, you said that it was Filipovic who had asked you to come and join the HVO. From what I understood, Filipovic was a former legionnaire, as was Kapular, as was Gotovina, as was Roso, and there are other men in the same case. Inside the HVO, weren't you a conglomerate of former legionnaires?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Filipovic was a sergeant in the Foreign Legion. Kapular was never part of the Foreign Legion. And Filipovic phoned me up when I was in Corsica to ask me whether I was prepared to come to Croatia, and I came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what about Ante Roso?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ante Roso was also a non-commissioned officer in the Foreign Legion. But as I was in the Foreign Legion, I never met him because we never served in the same regiments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, and everybody else in the courtroom. Good afternoon to the witness too. And just for the correctness of the record, I want to say that during my cross-examination on the 24th it said that I would continue my cross-examination. That was what was on the record, but I'd like to thank the witness and inform the Court that I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, and good afternoon to Mr. Skender and everybody else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Skender, before I ask you my first question --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I'd like to clarify a point, Your Honour, about time, the time I have at my disposal. If you recall on Wednesday, I think it was last Wednesday, my learned friend Ms. Senka Nozica informed you on behalf of both of us that the two -- that two defence teams were interested in cross-examining General Skender and that we would divide up the time that was allotted to us, which was 45 minutes, and that after holding consultations it is highly likely that we're going to need some additional time, too, in order to be able to clarify all the questions that we consider could be of benefit to this Court and could be answered by the general. So Ms. Nozica and I divide up the 45 minutes, and if my arithmetic is correct, we both have 22 minutes, 22.5 minutes, and so any other time would go -- would be deducted from the Petkovic Defence. Now, if possible, can we do it that way, and that if I need a few more minutes than the time I have at my allotment, may that be deducted from my overall time, by I would like to request that you allow me to use additional time and I think it will be of benefit to one and all in the courtroom and that we'll have some valuable information from Mr. Skender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, normally speaking, as you know, you -- Ms. Nozica and you have been granted 45 minutes. Ms. Nozica has had 31 minutes so far, which means that normally speaking you should only have 14 minutes left. If you exceed this time, this will be deducted from your overall time credit.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd like to support what me learned friend has just proposed. I don't think ten minutes should and problem, but I did ask that everything over 22.5 minutes be deducted from my time and everything over 22.5 minutes deducted from her time. I know that I did make that proposal and that we did adhere to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let's take our calculating machine. Since you've had 31 minutes and since you had 22 minutes and 30 seconds, this means that you have 9 minutes and 30 seconds which will be deducted from your time, and Ms. Alaburic will have 22 minutes and 30 seconds, and if she exceeds this will be deducted from her allotted time. Before coming to the hearing, it is important to do your math again to make sure you don't make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank my colleague Ms. Nozica and thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General Skender, before I ask you a few questions, let's just inform the Trial Chamber and our colleagues from the Prosecution and everybody else in the courtroom, have we met before during the proofing session?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And did I tell you of the topics I'd like to discuss with you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But before I ask you what I said I would be asking you, prompted by the questions raised by Their Honours today I have a few additional questions for you, and the first of those relates to the difference between General Praljak's testimony about the military police and what you have told us about the military police, what you told us in -- on Thursday, in fact. Now, General Skender, do you know that at the end of December 1993, a reorganisation took place of the military police, which scrapped brigade platoons and that the brigade military police was integrated into a brigade, and that the light assault battalions of the military police which were intended for combat were abolished as units of the military police, and the men were then transferred to the guards brigades. Are you aware of that, of the fact that the military police was organised in that fashion?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, since you arrived in Herceg-Bosna in July 1993, do you happen to remember, perhaps, when the name operative zone, for example, North-west Herzegovina, was changed and was called a military district of North-west Herzegovina and later on the military district of Tomislavgrad? Was that in the second half of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I believe it was in the second half.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Just one more question with respect to your testimony on Thursday, and what I am going to ask you about was recorded in the transcript on pages 45216 and 45217. Judge Antonetti asked you something and you said what a soldier, a commander would do if he were to learn that his soldier had committed a crime, that one of his men had committed a crime, and that Judge Antonetti asked you whether the military commander after handing the case over to the SIS or the military police, whether he has the responsibility of following the case up further and monitor and to see what happened and how the -- his -- his men were punished, and you said that he should be at least informed about what was going on with respect to the sanctions taken against one of his men. Now, my question to you, Mr. Skender, is this: Who is it who would have to inform the military commander about what was going on in an investigation undertaken against a soldier from his unit? Who has that responsibility and duty?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that the commander of the area needed to be informed, but I don't know who needed to inform him, because -- whether it was between the military authority or the civilian authority. In that case the commander of the area was no longer responsible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I would just like to make a -- a correction. To my surprise, without my having put the question to you, you said that when the brigade commander seized the competent body of this matter he needed to follow it through, and I was quite surprised by what you said. I didn't put the question to you. You yourself mentioned this. And Ms. Alaburic is now saying that this was a question I had put to you, which is not the case. This is something you said when you answered a question. And now when you answer you answer somewhat different yet again. You say that if a given body is seized of this or of a particular matter, the brigade commander has nothing to do with it anymore.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He's got nothing to do with it anymore. Once the military authorities is dealing with then he's got nothing to do with it anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are testifying under oath here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say one thing on the Thursday and when you say something else on the Monday, we would like to have an explanation for this. I -- I share the view of the President of this Chamber, who was very much surprised. You told us that he needed to be kept informed because he needed to follow it through.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once he had handed this over to the military police or to another authority, then he didn't need to follow it through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to be a contradiction here. Either he needs to check and make sure to see what has happened. You said if the order had been carried out -- maybe I got this wrong. I thought you said that the commander needed to make sure that the order had been carried out. When did you mean when you said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant is when a military commander gives an order dealing with a criminal affair concerning a particular individual to the military police, he then is to make sure that this person has been properly transferred to the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And who tells him? Who -- where does he get his information from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His command, to know whether the person's left or not. Otherwise, I don't see how else it can be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Skender, I will be using part of my time to try to show the Chamber that you are today telling us the same thing that you were telling us on Thursday in essence. Nevertheless, my understanding was that there was a certain degree of misunderstanding between the Trial Chamber and you. General Skender, at page 45216 we have the following recorded -- 45216 is the page number. You are recorded as saying that a military commander must react immediately to stop anything negative going on. He must also call in the military police and hand the case over to them. At 45217, we see this, and I'll quote in English. It's about the responsibility of the military commander. The General said: [In English] "He should at least be informed about what happens after. [Interpretation] General, I think that clarifies the matter. I would like to pursue my original line of questioning now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, General. I thank Ms. Alaburic for having tried to shed some light on this by just recalling what you said Thursday, but this doesn't solve everything. The -- say that the brigade commander will seize the military prosecutor, but let's imagine that the military prosecutor does nothing for some kind of reason that we don't know, even though a crime was committed. Now, according to you, do you think that the brigade commander must absolutely do something, or since the military prosecutor's not doing anything he decides to do the same thing and do nothing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to me he must do something. He must act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But what is he supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's supposed to arrest the person who committed the crime with the help of the military police he has under his ranks, in his brigade, and to gaol that person in the military gaol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, but your answer is making things even more complicated. Let me try to sum things up. Let's imagine that a crime was committed some place. The brigade commander is asking the military police to carry out an investigation. The military police does the investigation, writes the report, and sends its report to the military prosecutor, and Mr. X, Y, or Z, are the authors of the crime or the perpetrators, but the military prosecutor decides to do nothing, just stays idle. Now, you tell -- you're telling us that the brigade commander who followed the case, when he notes that the military prosecutor did nothing, that the investigative magistrate was not seized or did nothing also, then according to you, the brigade commander must arrest the perpetrator. Is this what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've never experienced such a case where the competent military authority did not react and did nothing. I said that the brigade commander should, but I've never experienced this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you don't have a hands-on case to tell us, but if it had happened, that was the way it was supposed to work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to me that's the way it was supposed to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'd like for the record and not to let any misunderstanding come up, say that as far as I'm concerned, these questions of law relate to the law applicable on the battle-field in Herceg-Bosna. The Court is not asking the witness to explain international public law to the court and to tell the Court what the law of command responsibility under Article 3 -- 7, paragraph 3 of the Statute means. That would not be appropriate because jura novit curia, we are supposed, and I think -- I hope rightly so, that we know the law. I just wanted to -- to make this clear so that no misunderstanding could come up when someone reads the records. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. However, General, when you answered my question, I would like to know when you answered in the position of a brigade commander wherever he may be, in Herceg-Bosna, Croatia, Beijing or anywhere, so was your answer a general answer stating what a brigade commander is supposed to do in such a case, whatever the country, or could you tell us whether the answer you gave us was very specific and only applicable to Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said what he was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What he was supposed to do wherever he may be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I had understood in your answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Skender, to pick up on this, I have several questions alone the same lines. You said you never encountered a case like that in Herceg-Bosna and you can hardly say what would be done in practical terms based on your knowledge. Is that a fair understanding of what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what about the three or four months, roughly speaking, your time as commander of the Tomislavgrad District? Did you familiarise yourself with the criminal laws and other applicable laws in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not familiarise myself with these documents because I didn't have any time. I was on the field day and night 'round the clock.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Would that mean that what you told us about the rules of behaviour that applied to a military commander result from your experience of what a military commander should be expected to do, and was that not a result of your experience both in the French Army and your direct experience upon your arrival in Bosnia and Herzegovina regardless of any regulations that might have applied?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, its my personal experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say "personal experience," do you mean your extensive experience in the French Army?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the French Army we didn't experience this kind of problem. Whenever something happened, it was automatically solved between the command and the gendarmerie. They would work it out together.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. General, let's try to go back to my original line of questioning. You are a professional soldier, and as such I wanted to ask you this: What in your opinion is the relationship between the army, on the one hand, professional soldiers, and the civilian authorities on the other? Is the army responsible for carrying out certain tasks regardless of which political party happens to be in power at a given time in a given country?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army must obey the politicians. The army must obey any political decisions made.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In your opinion as a professional soldier, is there a limit? How far should a soldier obey orders by civilian authorities? Will you always obey any orders by any civilian authorities no matter what as a professional soldier?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just like in any other armies. Whenever an order might lead to abuse against civilians, you are not supposed -- you're not forced to carry out this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, is it just about abuse against civilians, or perhaps does this definition entail other crimes and criminal offences as well?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any action that could be sanctioned. Any action that is banned by the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. So, for example, you receive an order to commit a crime. In your capacity as a professional soldier, it is your duty and responsibility to say, "No. I refuse." This runs counter to law. It's against the law; it's a crime. Is my understanding correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, during your time in Herceg-Bosna, was there ever a situation in which you received an order from someone to do something that might have constituted a crime or an offence?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. I'll be asking you several document-based questions next.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have the usher's assistance? I would like to show the witness a small set of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The first one up is an OTP exhibit, P11033. 11033. Again, P11033. It has now been recorded accurately. Thank you. The Prosecution used this document to finish their cross-examination of General Praljak. We can have a look together. This is an order by Brigadier Ivan Kapular, dated November 1993. The order is about punishing a number of soldiers for refusing to go to the southern front. Have you had a look, General? I've no questions about this document but about the southern front generally based on my following document. Could you please look at the next document then, please, 4D01293, item 2.1. It's a document signed by Croatia's defence minister, Gojko Susak. In March 1996. It's about mobilisation and deployment of Croatia's armed forces. The mobilisation plan of the armed forces. Item 1, Croatia's minister orders that the command of the southern front be abolished as part of the general mobilisation plan of the armed forces. Based on a document like this, it would seem, General Skender, that the southern front was indeed in Croatia and that there was such a thing as a command of the southern front that was part of the mobilisation plan of the Main Staff of Croatia's armed forces. General Skender, could you please tell us what you know about the existence of a southern front in Croatia's territory?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The southern front, I believe it went from Split to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That's fine. I just wanted to have that clarified for the Chamber's benefit. Now a question about an answer you gave about the confrontation lines and the army's responsibility vis-a-vis what was going on along the confrontation lines. I would like to show you a map now showing the Municipal Boarders across the Tomislavgrad district.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to interrupt, Ms. Alaburic. I'm a bit surprised. You talked about -- you talked about document P11033 and then said that you had no questions to put regarding this document. So why did you show it? Probably not to tender it because the witness said nothing about this document. It looks like you're wasting your time, but -- and now that I'm asking a question, we're wasting even more time. But maybe in the future, so I could understand better what you're doing, because I know counsels always do something with a reason, it would be nice if you could tell us what the reason was for showing this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was trying to save some time. I therefore omitted some information that may be significant. The last document is a document used by the OTP in their cross-examination of General Praljak. By using this document, the Prosecution were trying to prove that the southern front was in Herceg-Bosna and that the soldiers of the Croatian Army who refused to go to the southern front were subject to disciplinary measures. It was my mistake not to explain about that part of the cross-examination. We believe that this was an important matter, the matter being it was Croatia's army actually present in BH territory. If so, under what circumstances. I have now brought up this new document in a bid to show that the southern front was actually in Croatia. That was my intention, and I apologise if I was not sufficiently clear about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all the other microphones not being used please be switched off. We can't hear counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's now extremely clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the usher please hand this map to the witness. Can we have it placed on the ELMO. And then we'll have the witness point out a number of things to us. Could we please pull it up a little. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Skender, let's try to point out a number of things for the benefit of the Chamber. For example, Tomislavgrad municipality, and then we'll move on from there to Siroki Brijeg. What about Tomislavgrad? Was there an HVO Brigade in Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We're looking now at Tomislavgrad municipality, and can you please show where exactly the front line was along, which defence tasks were being performed by the Tomislavgrad Brigade? I'm talking about 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there in 1993. I only arrived at the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I wasn't there in 1992, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the Tomislav Brigade was towards Kupres. The line went towards Kupres, and there was always reinforced towards Prozor in front of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what about Tomislavgrad municipality specifically? Could you please use the marker and draw the front line that ran through Tomislavgrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was like this, if I remember right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you point out roughly for us where the town of Tomislavgrad was exactly within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was right there. About there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about the town itself? Was it covered by the area where the Tomislavgrad brigade was active? I'll repeat my question. Because I think it should be interpreted differently. Did Tomislavgrad find itself -- was the Tomislavgrad -- [In English] Was the Tomislavgrad situated on the area of combat activities of the HVO Tomislav Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no combat and no fighting in Tomislavgrad itself but only in the northern border and also towards Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Skender, can you look at Siroki Brijeg municipality now, please. What about the area of Siroki Brijeg municipality? Was there any combat going on there, or was there a confrontation line between your forces and the enemy, whoever the enemy happened to be?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: North of Siroki Brijeg there was a line that went through Mostar and that went south.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Skender, what about the area of Siroki Brijeg municipality itself?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no fighting in the Siroki Brijeg region.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, would it not be fair to say, then, for example, that in the area of Siroki Brijeg municipality the HVO Brigade had no defence tasks? Simply because there was no front line to speak of, there are no clashes with the enemy? Would that not be a fair description of what the municipal brigade had to do in the area of Siroki Brijeg municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. North of Siroki Brijeg there was a front-line against the Muslims, and they held these lines, probably. I don't know exactly how many men held these lines, but there were -- there was a line that went all the way to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was that the line that was already in the area of Mostar municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the line that followed the Neretva.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Thank you, General. I think we now understand about the front line. Could you now please use this map to place today's date on it, the 28th of September, 2009, and could you please initial the map. I will then be asking the registrar to have a number for this map.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] IC number please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Which date?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is today's date? 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Mr. President, good afternoon. Sorry to interrupt. Might the witness also date the map as to which date it's actually meant to represent in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, about the question posed by my learned friend from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record the document just marked by the witness shall be given Exhibit IC1052. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is a map with the front lines from August to December 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, at that time you were not on the field; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was south of Mostar at the time as a -- as observer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have said so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you weren't -- you didn't command any units yet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I had no command at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let us try to use another two documents to show the Chamber what the confrontation line was and the area in which the army was active. Could you please look at the next document in my set, 4D1364. 1364. This is a report signed by the commander of the Mostar defence sector, Zlatan Mijo Jelic. Let's look at this together. What exactly does this expression mean, the confrontation line in Mostar in the central part? There is talk here of the confrontation line Staklena Banka being held by the members of the Mostar police station, meaning civilian police. The line is being held by a total of 12 police officers. Along another line another 12 policemen are on standby. The question, General Skender, is this: The other line mentioned here, is that not the first or nearest fallback position, or is the meaning of this other line something entirely different? Could you please shed some light on that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to me, this can only be a fallback position.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And the next line is around the Stara Gimnazija or old school, held by members of the 1st Battalion of the military police, and then the third line is between the old secondary school, the Stara Gimnazija and the health centre, and that is held by an HVO battalion. And then we go on to the next line around the health centre held by members of the ATG or anti-terrorist group called Mrmak, and then another line from Aleksica Kuca to Zahum held once again by the HVO battalion, and each of those lines has reserve positions too. Tell me, General Skender, to the best of your knowledge this description given in the report for central Mostar and the confrontation line, does it correspond to what you have described to us here in court as being the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, when there's a document which is a military document, I then read it and I listen to your answer, and then I place this document against the background of the whole case. This is a document which I see for the first time. It hadn't made a marked impression on me so far. If I have understood correctly, this is an HVO document from the 1st Battalion of the military police in Mostar, dated 14th of July. The document states that there is a first line with 12 policemen and then a second line. What I'm interested in is what is mentioned afterwards. It seems that this document says that there's a sniper who is in a building, the Optika shop. Militarily speaking, if there is an enemy sniper somewhere, in military terms what must the other side do to neutralise this sniper or to annihilate him, without speculating, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the other side needs to place another sniper in order to neutralise the man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the HVO commander, if he is competent, must place a sniper to neutralise the other sniper. Do we agree on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's quite right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your answer is clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Skender, let's look at the next document now, please, which is 363. No. I apologise. 1364. The next document is 4D01364. 1364, yes. And it's a document by the same author. Let me repeat the document number. 4D1364 -- 63. 1363. Right. 1363, dated the 13th of July, the same author, sector commander, the defence of Mostar, Zlatan Mio Jelic, and we have there identical descriptions of the confrontation line in Mostar. Now, General Skender, would you take a look at the description for those lines and tells us whether this document corresponds to what we've heard from you here in the courtroom -- or, rather, did you describe the confrontation lines in the same way?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The combat lines went right through the city centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to ask you a few more questions, General Skender, about Prozor at the time when you were the commander of the military district of Tomislavgrad, and for us to do that let's look at the next document which is 4D1357. 4D1357. It's a document signed by Luka Markesic, the chief of the SIS headquarters in Rama, and it describes the situation in Rama along with an incident which took place on the 25th of February, 1994. Tell us, General, were you informed about this incident? Did you know about it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, since the Rama Brigade surrounded my command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that incident, but look at the next document first, please, and it's 4D1358. 4D1358. It's a document issued by you, General Skender, on forbidding the bearing of long-barrelled guns. Is this your order?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why you issued this order?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very simple. The men leaving the front line went home to Prozor, because generally speaking, this was the Rama Brigade, and I had prohibited them from going into town in light of the incidents that occurred on a daily basis in the bars.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now look at the next document 4D1456. Tell us, General Skender, did I give you a chance to read through that document after our talk last Wednesday, I believe?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's a plan of activities of the administration of SIS and the military police of the HVO to restore law and order in the Uskoplje Rama area. The document dates to 1994, March, and it was compiled by Mr. Marjan Biskic, and we've had an opportunity of meeting him here in the courtroom. Let's look at some of the elements of the plan of activities for the SIS administration of military police. In the third paragraph it says, and I'm going to paraphrase it, it's relatively difficult to establish law and order at a time when fighting is going on against the enemy forces. Was that your experience, too, that it was difficult to establish and control law and order and to control the general situation in town while there was fighting going on, while enemy activities were under way and fighting was going on?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It was very difficult to maintain law and order whilst fighting at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in the next paragraph, as a negative factor of this difficult situation, mention is made of a large number of mini units with self-proclaimed commanders who, throughout that time were in fact not subordinated to anybody, but joined the combat operations exclusively and in accordance to their own volition and assessment. Tell us now, General Skender, a description of the situation of this kind in this part of Herceg-Bosna, is it correct? Were there really these mini units with self-appointed commanders who were not subordinated to anybody?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. These were the small chiefs, as I call them, who had organised small combatant groups and who obeyed -- who were a law unto themselves, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, on the next page, General Skender, if we look at the fourth paragraph on the second page, the incident with you is mentioned. Anto Bradic, Banjaluka, under threat of arms, is being taken out. Anyway, General Skender, is that the event that you described to us in this courtroom about how you were taken into custody in this manner by this soldier?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I believe we talked about this on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It was Thursday, I think, yes. It don't matter. Yes. Now, General Skender, I'm going to ask you something now with respect to the statement you made to the Praljak Defence, and if I remember or understood you correctly, in your statement you try to explain that it was difficult to achieve the purpose for sanctioning and punishing a soldier, taking disciplinary measures against a soldier when there was fighting going on, and that there were certain situations where it was more important to use that soldier, who should otherwise be sanctioned, to be used in a combat in the unit. Can you tell me, to begin with, whether I understood that part of your statement correctly, or do you think I misunderstood it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You understood me perfectly well. It is very difficult to take men out of a combatting or fighting unit, to impose penalties, because it is quasi-impossible to impose sanctions straight away.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now take a look at the next document, General, which is P293.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, this document which we have before us is a document dated March 1994. Your command in Tomislavgrad was a command you exercised until when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I took up my command in December 1993, and I left in beginning of March 1994 because I had -- I was on leave and I went back to Corsica. I was then called by the minister of defence, Susak, who asked me to come to Zagreb and to be the second in command of the 1st Croatian Guards Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your command from December to March was Prozor part of your area of responsibility or command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have heard witnesses from Prozor who have told us a number of things. We have seen a great number of documents that demonstrate that in this Rama Brigade there was a whole series of problems. In this document we have before us now, the document states that there was this Kinder platoon which committed a whole series of acts against civilians, amongst other people. When you were in command was this something you were aware of or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was told that things had happened just the way you have just described them, but nobody ever came to file a complaint, whether it be civilians or military. Nobody came to me to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I don't wish to put you in a tricky situation. This is not my intention, but I need to do what I am here for, and I need to put into perspective a number of things which are mentioned in the indictment, and I need to ask you your opinion on a number of issues. In the indictment, it says that in December 1993, in Prozor, there were 500 to 600 Muslim civilians. In the indictment, it also says that at the end of December these civilians had been detained or sent to areas controlled by the ABiH or had gone abroad. On reading the indictment, one has the feeling that there were hardly any Muslim left in Prozor, and the few Muslims that had remained were detained. This is what the Prosecutor says in its submissions. Now, what is your position vis-a-vis the Muslim civilians? What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew that there were a number Muslim civilians in Prozor, but I didn't know how many there were there, and I knew even less whether they were going abroad or to other places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you yourself, did you go to Prozor? Did you visit the town or did you never go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in Prozor all the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you meet any Muslims or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the streets, very few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this was not a problem to see that there were hardly any Muslims in town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assumed that before my arrival they had either left, but I was not astonished not to see many Muslims there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General Skender, at that time -- if you could just describe the situation to us in Prozor. Was Prozor in fact chock-a-block full of soldiers, or was there an equal number of soldiers, civilians, and then Croatian civilians too? Well, generally speaking, who moved around the streets of the town of Prozor at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could see a great number of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And in the streets, for example, did you see civilians who were Croatian?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very few.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let's get back to that last document that I have prepared for you. P293 is the number, and they are Rules of Military Discipline. We haven't had an opportunity to go through them in any detail here in court yet, and, General Skender, you told us that you didn't have time to deal with rules and regulations, so let's just clear this situation up. I assume you haven't had time to read these rules on military discipline either; is that right? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Never mind. Let's take a look at Article 7 anyway. "Decisions on Military Discipline." It is the penultimate page of this document, and I'd like to draw your attention to several articles. In Article 102, and I quote, it says: "Discipline measures and punishments which, given the circumstances and conditions of their administration, cannot be carried out or whose carrying out would be purposeless shall not be pronounced in wartime." And its in the section "Decisions on Disciplinary Reliability in Wartime." So that's the quotation. And then we have Article 105, para 3, which reads as follows, and I quote: "Disciplinary measures of military detention or disciplinary punishment of detention shall be suspended or postponed if so required by the tasks of the unit, i.e., the institution or for reasons of security and protection of individuals as described in para," et cetera, in para 2 of this article. And one more provision. That is to say Article 109, para 1. It says: "If the individual against whom a military punishment has been pronounced shows courage or distinguishes himself in service, the disciplinary punishment may be reduced, mitigated, or remitted." Now, since the measures and punishment could have been proclaimed by a court or -- what we've just read out as being a rule, does that coincide with what you were talking about when it came to priorities when looking at punishment and when there's combat under way? Is that along the lines of what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with these rules, but I applied it to the letter as the rule states. I applied it to Banjaluka. In other words, the punishment of the person in question was postponed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, to make sure that everything is clear, as far as disciplinary measures are concerned, these are usually taken by the brigade commander; isn't that right? Do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it comes to small sanctions, yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as far as disciplinary measures are concerned, which are a more serious matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is referred then to the military police, for the military police to conduct its investigation and understand exactly what has happened or what's behind it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me give you a theoretical example. A soldier that has burnt down a house, for instance, when he has not received an order to burn down the house; so a soldier that kills a civilian, for instance; a soldier that rapes a woman; a soldier that takes a car, the television set, and the fridge of another person; and so on. According to you, this type of behaviour, is this something which would require a disciplinary measure to be taken by the brigade commander, or does this kind of behaviour need to be referred to another authority other than the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This should be referred to the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In light of the seriousness of the military situation, the military police, as far as you are concerned, don't you think it should arrest the offender and despite the military's situation it should, don't you think, arrest the offender or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was supposed to arrest the offenders, but in light of these rules, this could be postponed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your interpretation of the text we have before us, in certain cases do you think that the military police can postpone the arrest because of the military situation, which means that there is a reason, a valid reason to, postpone the arrest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think it does, but it still investigates into the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that completes my cross-examination, actually. I'd just like to thank General Skender for his answers and thank you, Your Honours, for giving me additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is now 20 to -- quarter to 4.00. We shall have our break now, and after the break the Prosecutor will start his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours, and to all in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, General Skender. May I just first of all please, and I'll be clear with you, about how came to be in Herzegovina in the summer of 1993. All right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived in Zagreb --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm just introducing the topic. I'm going to ask you the questions in short pieces so we that understand each other clearly as we go. No, it's my fault. I want to look at it in two parts, please, Mr. Skender. First of all, coming to Croatia, number one; and then number two, going to Herzegovina as you told us, to Citluk. All right? Yes?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I arrived in Croatia at the end of June, in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to cut you off. Again, it's my mistake. I'm just introducing the topic to you. I just want to make sure I've got it clear with you. There was a Croatian officer who you had met in the Foreign Legion who contacted you and who asked if you wanted to give a helping hand to the Croatians to defend their country; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. And he was called Filipovic. Is that also right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. Once you were in Croatia, you were then asked by someone from the Ministry of Defence if you would volunteer to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that also right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Someone from the Ministry of Defence. Not the minister of defence but someone from the entourage of the Ministry of Defence, and I said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes. And just so that we're clear, that was my question: You were asked by someone from the Ministry of the Defence if you would volunteer and that's the position, yes?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I guess it was someone from the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Were you in contact with General Praljak at all before going to Croatia or to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: He had no involvement at all in your deployment to Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to read to you and to everybody else a short passage from the evidence that General Praljak gave on June the 18th of this year, sitting where you were. It's page 41645, at line 14, and the General was being asked questions by His Honour Judge Antonetti, particularly about members of the armed forces of Croatia who had gone to fight in Bosnia. All right? And one of the things that General Praljak said about that was in relation to you. He said -- I think it's possible to show it on the screen. I think it's on the screen. The question is at line 11 to do with officers in the army of Croatia who are part of the HVO and who had volunteered but who still remained, from a military standpoint, part of Croatia. And General Praljak said this: "That's what I claim, Your Honour. And I know for sure that Mr. Skender ... well he's a French national and lives in Corsica, and I contacted him and he expressly asked to go to the battlefront and into the HVO as a volunteer to Bosnia-Herzegovina." Just hold on a moment. I'm going to ask you a question now. Those two versions of how you came to be in Bosnia are very different, are they not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember General Praljak contacting me. I repeat, someone from the ministry of defence in Croatia contacted me asking me whether I would volunteer to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes, you said that. I want to, if I may, ask you the question again with respect. The two versions are quite different, aren't they? One has you coming, Filipovic having spoken to you, then the Ministry of Defence; the other is Mr. Praljak apparently contacting you and you volunteering to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Just a moment. I want to -- I've asked a question, I wonder if the witness could answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, just a minute. Do not raise an objection right away just to interrupt. The Prosecutor is doing his job. He's noting that there is a discrepancy and he's asking the witness about it. What do you want to take the floor for?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nonetheless, Your Honours, before I place an objection on the record, given your remark I believe that the witness, without wanting to lead the witness to say or think anything, the Prosecutor and the witness are not talking about the same thing. These are two different representations, and in my attempt -- and in my opinion an attempt to mislead the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we'll see clearly where we're going once the Prosecutor is done with this line of questioning. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I can assure that -- everybody I'm not intending to mislead a person, particularly not the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The quotation that I read from -- from the transcript appears to suggest that General Praljak is saying he was the one who contacted you and he was the one who asked you if you would come and you volunteered to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what the transcript appears to show, General Skender, and I'm asking you to confirm whether in your recollection of these matters that is wrong, for they cannot both be correct, can they?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's wrong. Let me repeat. I got a call from Mr. Filipovic in Corsica. I arrived in Croatia and that's when Bugojno fell, and someone from the Ministry of Defence asked me. I don't know who it was, I don't know his name, but asked me whether I would volunteer to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: To Herzegovina interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may just add a question. Is it possible, Mr. Skender, that the person from the ministry was Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. I don't think that it was Praljak. I really don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Because you would remember if General Praljak was the person from the ministry. So far from misleading anybody, can we leave it like this, General Skender: You can't help us at all with these two different accounts. You can't help us with why there should to be two different accounts of you coming to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I -- I maintain with -- I maintain what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Would you look with me, please, on this topic at the statement that you provided to the Praljak Defence and look at page 2, please, in the English, at page 4 in the B/C/S. Can you find on page 4 -- ah, you're going to need some help. I think the statement is right at the back of the Praljak bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I wonder if the usher could assist. Or right at the front, in fact, in that one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: That's the statement that you provided, I think, to the Praljak Defence. Could you look at the fourth page of that statement in the Croatian, please, and find the paragraph that deals with you deciding to help to create -- help and defend an independent Croatian state. It's at the top of page 4 in the Croatian. Can you see a paragraph that reads: "Being a born Croat and a retired officer of the French Army observing what was going on in the former Yugoslavia ...," can you see that? And the next paragraph starts: "In the summer of 1993..." Can you see those two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it, "Being a born Croat." I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So the paragraph that has "Being a born Croat," ends with these words: "I had decided to return to Croatia to help defend and create an independent Croatian state." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And the next line says: "In the summer of 1993, I went to Herzegovina where the Muslim-Croat conflict had been going on." Can you also see that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: By the summer of 1993, Croatia had declared its independence and been recognised by the United Nations, had it not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And Bosnia-Herzegovina, likewise.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And you were in Bosnia fighting the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't -- I didn't see things from that angle. I was here to help the Croatian people who were fighting against the Muslims at the time. I had no afterthought whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, General Skender, there aren't two ways of looking at it are there? You were helping the troops who were put into the field by the HVO to fight the troops who were put into the field by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is there another way of looking at it that -- that is exercising your mind? It's just that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not see things as you're telling them. I was there to defend the Croatian people who was fighting the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, one thing escaped me and I thank Mr. Laws for highlighting this. There is a terrible sentence in this document. You said that you came to create an independent Croatian state. This is a very important sentence. When you made your statement, did you write it in Croatian or did you write it in French?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You wrote it in Croatian. And you're fluent in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Croatian when you write "to create an independent Croatian state," what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Croatia, but I made a mistake, because Croatia had already been recognised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because when you read the sentence as it is, any reasonable trier of fact can very well say he's coming there to create within the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina an independent Croatian state. You can really see things from this angle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it could be interpreted in such a manner but it was not my intent at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're absolutely sure? You're under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, under oath, I'm absolutely sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to suggest to you for you to consider that the reality, the reality of the situation that you and others like you were in was that you knew that it was in Bosnia-Herzegovina that the borders of Croatia were being drawn. That is the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I repeat. I maintain what I said. I went to Herzegovina to help the Croatian people, but without any idea, a separation or any other idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Very well. We're going to move on now to look at the evidence that you have given to this Court in respect of discipline problems within the HVO. All right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, General, you're saying that there were very bad discipline problems within the HVO. That's the first proposition from your evidence, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And secondly, it was very difficult to deal with this situation, because the priority was keeping men available for combat.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: If you put them in prison, you reduce the numbers available for combat, and you also, and I think this might be an additional part of your evidence, you risk upsetting their fellow soldiers who might not want to fight alongside you anymore. That's also part of it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. As I repeat, all these people were volunteers and only volunteers. So if you sent one of them to gaol, there were always some of his friends or buddies who decided not to go to the front line anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. Well, we're going to come back to volunteers in a minute, but the background to these problems is a shortage of manpower, isn't it? A shortage of people to deploy in your front line. That's what it comes down to.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And although it was inevitable that law and order had to suffer, the choice was made that people should not be punished.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't always the case, but, yes, most of the time it was the case. For example, when you had deserters who did not answer the call-up to go up to the front line, were not sanctioned, but they were just -- once they were recaptured they were sent to the front line but without being sanctioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to ask you about deserters as a specific category of people committing what might be called crimes, but as a general proposition, if you don't punish the criminal, he is likely to carry on committing crime. Do you think that's fair?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I'm talking about deserters --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: No -- I'm sorry. I'm not talking about deserters. I'm talking about people who are committing crimes against civilians, people who are raping women, as we're going to look at in due course, people who are committing murders, crimes being committed against civilians. The men who were doing that, if you leave them free, they are likely to carry on, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my command in Tomislavgrad, I never experienced such a case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Very well. We'll look at that too. Now, volunteer army is something that you have been stressing. Badly trained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A follow-up question first. The Prosecutor is putting questions to you, questions which I've already put to you, but I think he's going further into details. We have seen a good number of officers here to testify, but you are one of the only officer with a dual experience. You already fought a war in Algeria, and then you fought a second war, quote unquote, war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So you have a dual experience, and there aren't that many officers who have been through two wars. Starting from this, we know that you've been in the military career for several years in -- during the Algerian war, and I'm sure that during this war in Algeria you must have experienced a number events which you experienced again in Bosnia-Herzegovina, notably the problem with deserters.
