We say, say that the Foreign Legion in Algeria were -- were all people who came from Indochina and that there was a good number of deserters at the time. So I am sure that you are well aware of this problem of desertion. As far as you recollect, what happened in Algeria when a deserter was recaptured? Was he sent to gaol or was he sent to the front line to fight.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Foreign Legion most desertions occurred during the training, and once the deserter was recaptured he was sent to gaol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you never experienced a situation where you had a deserter who was incorporated in a combat unit as a sanction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never experienced that in the French Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, should we -- I was going to deal with this topic later, but as it's been raised, shall we turn to deal with the question of desertion now and look in the binder that you've just been given, in the new binder, at document 4D01655, and I think it's the last document in the binder. Right at the very, very back, General. It's document dated the 11th of October 1993, and signed by Bruno Stojic. And I don't want to take up too much of our time with it, but we can see from the very first paragraph of the order that it directs the district military courts and district military prosecutor's office to give priority to cases related to the failure to respond for general mobilisation and to wilful abandonment of military units. All right? So can you see that, paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading. I'm reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. Well, you won't need to read all of it. Does that accord with your recollection of how things were, that the district military courts and the district military prosecutor's offices were specifically told that the priority was to deal with cases relating to failure to respond to the general mobilisation call and to people who had abandoned their units?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see this document, but all deserters, all military people who did not answer -- respond to the call were recaptured by the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes. And what I'm going to suggest to you is that it shows us that where the vital interests of the HVO are concerned, it is possible to set priorities.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see this priority. All I was -- all I am saying is that soldiers who failed to respond to the call were recaptured by the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: If you go back one document in the binder to 3D02798, we can see a document also from October of 1993 which has some orders to give about people who abandon their positions and defence lines. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And it says that the sanction is going to be shooting of the unit, 1(a). "Commanders of the units are to be proclaimed traitors of the people and convicted by the most severe punishment, which is shooting before the unit." Can you see that at 1(b)?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see this written.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So the suggestion being made by this deputy commander is that where the offence relates to people who have abandoned the front line, the suggestion is that they should be shot. Can you see that? That's what it's saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it seems to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So to go back to the issue of crime and law and order, some things that the soldiers do are going to be met with very severe punishment indeed, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- it's written, but that's not the way it was to be, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Generally speaking. All right. But we don't see, do we, a reaction of that kind to the Kinder Vod or to Ante Bradic, also known as Banjaluka. We're going to talk a little bit about them in a moment. The crimes that they might be committing are not dealt with in this way, are they?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the Kinder Vod, but as far as Banjaluka was concerned, it was sanctioned but it's true that the sanction was postponed, but the military court did eventually punish the perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I want to ask you about that. You told us on Thursday that you were told that shortly after you went back to Zagreb that Banjaluka had been sanctioned for this crime that he committed against you. Do you recall saying that on Thursday?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that. I was even asked whether I wanted to withdraw my complaint, but I said no and everything went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And when had you returned to Zagreb so that can try to date this information about Banjaluka being prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left for France early in March, and when I -- I was -- when I came back to Zagreb, I was -- I was detached to another unit of the Croatian Army. When I came back to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. Well, we're going to look at a couple of documents in relation to that. Let's go back to that day. Ante Bradic had the nickname Banjaluka, and we can see from document 3D00414 that the date is the 12th of January of 1994. All right? And it's important for us to have that date clear. So if you come back from the document you're on just four tabs backwards, you'll come to 3D00414. If you go back four tabs in that binder we can find the date without difficulty. 12th of January. All right? As you describe in your statement -- if you want to follow it in your witness statement it's page 3 in both languages, the last paragraph. What he did that day involved him firing a gun at the ceiling of the refectory that you were in. You thought he had been taking drugs whilst he was doing that, and then he took you away at gunpoint. That's a summary of what happened on the 12th of January, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, except it was an assault rifle and not a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: An assault rifle. Thank you. On the face of it, it was an extremely serious thing for him to have done and also exceptionally dangerous. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was dangerous. He could have killed people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: In -- in the Foreign Legion, for example, what would the punishment had been for opening fire in one's own refectory then kidnapping a commanding officer at gunpoint and driving him away?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you'd go to the military court, prosecuted to the military court, and immediately arrested by the gendarme.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Let's look together, then, at what happened in his case, and if you turn to P11015. And from the document that you were on, it's back just two tabs. If you go back two tabs, General, you'll find P11015. Very short document signed by you. You haven't been shown it so far in your evidence, but it will help us. I'm so sorry. From the document that you were on in the binder. It's the last one with a P on it if that helps. It's further in than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I wonder if the General could be given some assistance, please. It's not an easy binder to find one's way around. It's the last P document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: That's really a two-line document in which you agree to postpone the arrest and taking into custody of Mr. Bradic, also known as Banjaluka, until the operation Tvigi 94 is finished since that operation is currently in process; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And that was an operation which was offensive or defensive, Tvigi 94?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Which I'm right in saying didn't, in fact, succeed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually it never started because there was a shortage of troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: That's exactly right. There was a shortage of troops and you couldn't get this operation off the ground. But in order to try to give it a chance, you were prepared to allow Banjaluka, for example, to be free, yes?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I -- by freeing Banjaluka or by locking up Banjaluka, at least that way I made sure that about 20 troops didn't leave the unit, that they stayed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. Turn over to the next document, please, in your binder, which is -- I'm so sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Do you plan to go on with Banjaluka?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: We're going to stay with Banjaluka for a few more documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The next one is the very next document in the binder, General. So from the page you're on now, if you turn to 3D00414. 3D00414.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, that's my mistake. I've misled. The very next document is the one I mean, it's 3D00113, not 114. So back one document, do forgive me. The document dated the 20th of June of 1994 from Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: For the record, it may be useful to state that it is document 3D01098. Is that correct, Mr. Laws?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. The transcript didn't show what Your Honour said. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: No, it's 3D00113.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And if we look at the foot of that page, I think we can see that Ante Bradic, also known as Banjaluka, describes how he captured you, shooting over your head, and how he has still not been brought into custody to this day. Can you see that? This is June of 1994, some five months after this incident and after you've been to Zagreb, as you've told us.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not familiar with these documents, but I'm sure that Banjaluka, at least that was -- I had been told, had been punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, the author of this document appears to take a different view in June of 1994; namely, that nothing's been done about him. He's just still a free man at liberty to create any sort of trouble that he likes.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Were you aware that he had already been in trouble once before and already once before escaped punishment?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt my dear colleague, but could you please enlighten us where exactly in this document is passage you're referring to? It's a multipage document, and I don't know whether the witness found it. You never made any reference to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It's at the foot of page 1 in the English, a paragraph beginning: "Ante Bradic, aka Banjaluka, captured the commander of the Tomislavgrad ZP, Colonel Zvonimir Skender. Took him at gunpoint to the Rama Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It's -- I'm so sorry, it is a Praljak document, but I should have pointed it out to you and I apologise for that. I hope that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Laws, could you give us the source for a previous misdeed of Mr. Banjaluka which you had just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm going to show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: -- the Court some documentation to that straight away. It's P04836. And again I think it might help if the general has some assistance with this. P04836.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: This would have happened not very long after you arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina, General, and we can see it's a criminal report about the same man, Ante Bradic, also known as Banjaluka. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And under the heading criminal report we have a paragraph about his background which doesn't concern us. The next paragraph says that in May and June of 1993, on unknown dates, he did two things, and we'll look at them separately. He transported persons of the Muslim faith from Prozor to Gornji Vakuf and Bugojno without permission from the competent organs in order to acquire illegal material benefits. Look at that. And two, that he illegally traded in weapons which he owned illegally. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not mentioned in the document I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: P04836, I think, is the one that does have those words in it.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: 836. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Can you see in the middle of the page the words "Criminal report"? In big letters, "Criminal report."

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Then there's the paragraph which starts "Against Ante Bradic, aka Banjaluka..." Don't worry about that paragraph just read the next paragraph which tells you the two things that he's trouble for. All right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And then if you -- if you come down two paragraphs from that paragraph you can see we get a little more detail about who the people who are being transported are. The above-named transported women of the Muslim faith from Prozor to Gornji Vakuf charging a hundred Deutschmarks, making six trips. And then the last paragraph tells us that he also traded in weapons illegally, rifles, pistols, and other sidearms. All right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that and it doesn't surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: No. And he gets -- it doesn't surprise you because from your short but illuminating experience with Mr. Banjaluka. He was a thoroughly dangerous man, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, let's not worry about it too much. Can you help us, please, with -- with this: The women who were being transported by him, were you aware that there were any restrictions in place at any time in 1993 restricting the movement of Muslims in this area?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You were not aware that there were such restrictions and that people were effectively turning to people smuggling to try to make money out of their situation?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that because I was south of Mostar, not in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, I think you -- I think you told us that you did some touring of the front as well, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I was south of Mostar, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Very well. If you turn on, and we'll do this so that it's easy for you, I hope, because I know it's not a straightforward binder. 4836 is the one we're on. If you turn with me to P05889. You'll need to turn just three tabs from where you are now and you'll be on 5889. All right? I'm going to give you just a moment to read that document, particularly the part headed "Statement," and then we'll have a look at it together. All right? If you want to read it to yourself. We all have it in front of us. It deals with his account of being freed in respect of the charges we've just looked at of people smuggling and arms dealing.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see that he was held in the Heliodrom and that he was asked to pay out a lot of money.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And he was freed as a result of agreeing to join the Convicts Battalion, and he fought in Rastani on the 22nd of September of 1993. You saw that as well, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know where Rastani is, and I heard about Kazanicka Vojna [phoen], but I don't know in what circumstances this took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, all right. The man who kidnapped you in January of 1994 had -- I'm going to use a colloquial phrase, had the slate wiped clean for him in September by agreeing to join the Convicts Battalion and was fighting the very next day for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I read this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And if you go back two documents to P5303 -- P05303 I should have said. If you go backwards from where you were two documents. We see -- do you have that, General?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the document dated the 23rd of September?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: That's the one. We see that Bruno Stojic is citing for extraordinary valor the Convicts Battalion and Tuta in respect of the fighting at Rastani amongst other places. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So if we put all of that together, the policy of tolerating crime --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Counsel. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I let the witness respond to the question from my learned friend, but I really do have to object to this kind of examination where my colleague is trying to use this situation with this particular man, Ante Bradic, nicknamed Banjaluka, and the fact that he left prison to bring this -- to connect this with the commendation from Mr. Bruno Stojic, and that is unacceptable based on the documents. I'm going to be quite precise: In document P5889, this man, Banjaluka, says that from Heliodrom prison -- that he left Heliodrom prison on the 21st of September, 1993, and that on that same day he joined the Convicts Battalion. The commendation from Mr. Bruno Stojic is dated the 23rd of September, 1993, and refers to an operation, namely the BH Army attack on Rastani, Vrda, and Mostar, which we have shown during Mr. Praljak's cross-examination pursuant to orders for attack from the BH Army, and that is document P5079, and a report by the chief of PUPD HVO, Ciro Grubesic, and the number of that is 2D338, and even if under 2D338 -- or, rather, even if we were not to rely and refer to those documents, it is clear -- the question is clear. How could Mr. Bruno Stojic know that somebody, two days prior to that, prior to his commendation, joined some unit? Now, if the Prosecutor wishes to demonstrate that, then he had to connect these two documents, the documents he's referring to. In this way, he's just leaving the impression in court that Mr. Stojic knew that the person in question, Banjaluka, joined the Convicts Battalion and took part in these events. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, that's not an impression that I've created in the slightest, with the greatest of respect. What I've done is to show that Banjaluka took part in an attack on the 22nd of September, which is referred to in the document P05889, and it is that incident that Mr. Stojic cites for its valor the following day. I'm not suggesting that Stojic knows Banjaluka personally. It's to demonstrate that within the HVO the Convicts Battalion is recognised as being unit. Banjaluka is therefore in a recognised unit, and therefore we have, as I am going to put it to this witness, in effect, revolving doors on the prison. We go in, we come out, we fight. That's the point of it. The objection not to something -- to an impression that I've created at all. If my learned friend fears that there is of that kind coming, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise, but it seems that the Prosecutor is attempting in an identical manner to bring this -- to connect the two, because the Prosecutor now says that Banjaluka was a member of the Convicts Battalion, and in document P5889, which are the minutes of his interview, and in paragraph 2 he says that he joined up on the 21st of September, 1993, that he joined the Convicts Battalion then, and that was my objection. That is to say, two days before the document in which Bruno Stojic is commending the Convicts Battalion. So Mr. Bruno Stojic, even if he knew each and every combatant of the Convicts Battalion, certainly could not have known who joined this unit -- a person who joined the unit two days before he issued this document of his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I am not going to go into the details of Mr. Stojic, which is ancillary at the moment. Well, we have a soldier who has been gaoled on the 23rd of September, 1993, in the Heliodrom, and lo and behold on the 21st of September an officer whose name he quotes, Bozo, who belongs to the Convicts Battalion, comes to see him in prison and says to him, "If you join us, there will be no disciplinary measures, no sanctions imposed on you. These will be annulled." He agrees to it, but he's not the only one who agrees to it, because in -- in the next paragraph we can see at that there are 20 or so men who join the Convicts Battalion. He goes to the battlefront, and then on the 23rd of September, he will be congratulated. This is what the document we have before us says. When I see that and then I see what happened to you when this famous Banjaluka in the refectory threatened you, takes your revolver and takes you to the Rama Brigade. We don't know why, but perhaps you will tell us why. This soldier named Banjaluka, who moves around in total impunity since he has been asked to go and join the Convicts Battalion and what happens or what has happened will be set aside. Do you believe in your position that this is normal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not at all normal. I knew nothing about his past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why were you taken hostage by him? Why were you taken to the Rama Brigade? What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once I was in the Rama Brigade, he told me that in town someone had taken his pistol off him, and after that he was told that the order had been given by the commander of the area, i.e., me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After an incident of this kind where the top man in the area, and I would say was ridiculed by a mere soldier, if this is not sanctioned, don't you think this wouldn't discredit the army? Don't you think this weakens the command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, Your Honour. Yes. This is a way of discrediting the commander. But in light of the situation, I needed all my soldiers at the time because we were preparing an offensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that you had rather not impose a sanction on him straight away because you needed him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, Your Honour. Nonetheless, the case was referred to the military police who then prosecuted him afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You knew nothing about his past in the Convicts Battalion. You knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew nothing about that. It's the first time I hear about it today, as I read this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two questions for you, Witness. First of all, did you try to find out what had happened afterwards or whether there had been any proceedings against this person or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember exactly when, but I had been asked whether I wanted to withdraw my criminal report, and I was told that he had been tried and sanctioned. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell us exactly when you heard about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe this was around the month of June in 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. When this man named Banjaluka entered the mess, were you alone there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were a lot of men there, and everyone was armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you take any measures against the other people who, in a cowardly way, enabled this to happen and didn't do away with the man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave the order, and I said that no one should shoot. Had people started shooting, a lot of people would have got hurt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe you have told us -- told this already. I'm sorry, Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: See, as I understand the effect of the evidence that you've been asked to give here, it is to say to us that it was very difficult to impose law and order because the area was full of criminals.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: But if the policy that's being pursued is not to prosecute them or to let them go as soon as you catch them, then it's fair to say, isn't it, it's no good you saying that to us. This is a problem entirely of the making of the HVO, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this was a more general problem, but whatever the case may be, in the Prozor area this is how things were. There was a lot of corruption. There was a lot of other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. The other episode that you've been asked to talk about involves an incident that started in a cafe and involved two units ending up in a fight and people being shot, and that's in February of 1994. Do you remember that? You've told us about it on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And if we look together at 3D00113, which is the document we looked at in which -- dated June of 1994 in which we learned that Banjaluka hadn't been prosecuted by June, but it also has something to say about this episode in February.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I think General Praljak wants to attract the attention of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, they're not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [In English] It's okay? [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Can everybody hear now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: In the second paragraph of that document we have a description of what's called the well-known event of the 25th of February of 1994, which deals with this same incident, a clash in the town of Prozor between the Garavi unit from Bugojno and the Kinder Platoon in which two members the Kinder Platoon were killed. And on that occasion members of the Kinder Platoon also arrested a minister in the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Zuljevic. And that's the incident that you described which led to your barracks being surrounded and you deploying the military police. All right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This was part of my area of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It's the very next month after you have been taken prisoner, and I'm going to suggest to you that it has some obvious similarities. People are firing weapons and somebody appears to have been kidnapped in this incident well.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You don't know anything about the man who's been, as it's put here, arrested, the minister that's taken by the Kinder Platoon?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of a person being kidnapped in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. What you do have knowledge of is the way in which a lawless bunch of young men came to your headquarters with weapons and surrounded it, yes?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And you were able to call-out the military police to deal with the situation, and you were also able to enlist the help of General Praljak; is that also right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Military -- the military police arrived quickly, and the general also arrived pretty quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: One of the units involved in that disturbance was the Kinder Platoon, and you said it, I think a few moments ago, that you were not even aware of the name of the Kinder Platoon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that -- I had never heard about this Kinder Vod. I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The Kinder Vod were a lawless bunch of young men who fought for the HVO but also committed offences against the civilian population. You say you were not aware even of their existence?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that the Kinder Vod existed. I knew that they were fighting with the HVO. Now, as to the abuse they committed, I knew nothing of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, we've heard evidence given in this courtroom about them being a group of men who, for example, raped Muslim women in the houses at Prozor where the Muslim women had been kept separately in Duge. Were you at any time aware, General, that Muslim women had been kept in houses away from their menfolk?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I wonder if you'd look with me, please, at document P04307. If you go to the front of the binder, it's, I think, the seventh document in. And this document, I should say straight away, is under seal, as is the next one. If you can find the paragraph that starts -- it's about the seventh paragraph in: "We have also been informed that the Muslims in Prozor have all been moved into three areas of the region." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm kindly asking my dear colleague to take the number of paragraph first. There are a couple of chapters in this document. It should be -- be easier for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The last numbered paragraph is "Humanitarian activity," number 4, but after that they don't have numbers. So if we count on from that paragraph, can you see "4. Humanitarian Activity"?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance. The paragraph that my learned friend has in mind, General Skender, is on page 2 of the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's paragraph 4 looking from the top of the page down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm grateful to counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It's the fourth paragraph both counting from the top and up from the bottom. And I'm not going to read the whole thing out. You're capable of reading it yourself, General, but you can see the last sentence of that paragraph says that there are indications that HVO soldiers come into the area at night and rape the women they wish. Can you see that? All the men between 16 and 60 are gone. They're very frightened as to their future. Can you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think it would be fair for the witness if -- if he would be first asked a question about whether he was there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, I think first we'll ask him to read the document, and then we'll take it from there if we don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, but then attention on the date of the document should be -- okay. Certainly that would be normal procedure, but however ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you have four professional Judges sitting on this Bench and they note all this. No need to stand up to say all this. I mean, we're no fools. We understand. We know very well that in August 1993 the witness was not in command. Just let Mr. Laws put his questions and we'll see. Please resume, Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I may have been overly-hasty. I said it would be fair to show the witness the document, not the Chamber. Of course the Chamber is bound to see the document, as have I. The proper thing to do would be to ask the witness first whether he was there at the time. In order to do that first, he would have to state the date, but if he wants to go straight to the heart of the matter, well, he might as well do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: In August of 1993, there were Muslim women who had been confined to a number of houses in villages in the Prozor area, and they were being raped. One of the units that took part in those rapes was the Kinder Vod, and witness -- a witness here in this court, a Witness BN, has given evidence about that. So I'm giving you, if you like, General Skender, some background information. The Kinder Vod you said you knew to be troops who fought for the HVO. They acted with impunity in this area, did they not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. Maybe so, but I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I should have put a question to you, but I forgot to do so. In December when you took over your command, the command of this operational zone, who were you replacing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was replacing Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Siljeg, could you tell us whether he handed over the command? Officially, did you meet with him and did he brief you on the situation, or was he already gone when you arrived.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't brief me. He left for his new post without telling me anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But Siljeg must have had deputies. Could -- did you ask that -- his deputies to at least brief you on the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked his deputies to brief me on the situation on the front line, to brief me on the situation on the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But no one at that time told you that there were big problems in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, but I knew about it, because I noted right away that there were very important command problems, very serious command problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you didn't know about the rapes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, this is a document under seal, so I will not say who wrote it or where it came from, but I thought I understood that international representatives had sent liaison officers, and the international representatives would say to the liaison officers, This is what's happening, and normally the liaison officer was supposed to feedback this information up to the command. Is that the way it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my zone there was a British Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. A British Battalion in your zone. So there was liaison office. There must have been a Croatian liaison officer with this battalion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I don't remember his name, but this person did exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as this document we have, document which was written before your arrival, so I'm not going to ask you what you were -- what you should have done. I'm going to ask you a theoretical question. There is a report of this situation made in August. I assume that normally in any army worthy of this name the foreign commander should have told the liaison officer, "Listen, there's a very serious situation on the ground."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I suppose that they must have told them so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when you took your command, did the British commander come to meet with you to take stock of the situation with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He came to introduce himself. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he never told you, "We've heard, we know that a number things happened"? He said nothing of this sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And it wasn't just the internationals who knew. SIS knew all about it as well. Let's look at one of their reports, P04177. It's five documents in from the beginning of the folder. If you go right from the beginning and count five you'll be there. It's page 2 of the English. It's page 1 in the B/C/S, General Skender. It's the final paragraph on page 1 in the Croatian, and it deals with exactly the same finding as the internationals that we've just looked at. Can you see the final paragraph every day, women and girls are taken out from the collection centres at Podgrade, Lapsunj, and Duge, which are not secure, taken to houses where they are raped. Can you see that? And it deals with other humiliations as well, which I needn't go into. Do you see those words written by the SIS officer, Luka Markesic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the document, but I didn't have time to read it in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You don't need to read it in full. I'm dealing with one part in which it's clear, I'm going to suggest to you, that the SIS officer writing this report in August of 1993 is spelling it out, that SIS know exactly what's happening within these collection centres to these women. That's all you need from that document. Are you saying that you never heard about this when you took over from Siljeg who was commander at this stage? You're saying no one ever mentioned it to you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one told me about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, when you took over your command in the operational zone, could you tell us whether in the operational zone command there was a person from SIS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he didn't brief you to say in August there was a report, nothing is happening? This is happening. Now that you're here, we hope that you're going to do something about it. He said nothing of this sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if he had told you so, what would you have done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would have tried to solve the problem, you know, with the meager possibility I had, but I must repeat I was absolutely not aware of any of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: But they weren't meager possibilities. Let's leave you out of the picture. Anybody in a command position in this area could have done what you did when there was a problem at the cafe that ended up at your barracks. Call out the military police. Have the place surrounded. That was an option that you exercised in the example that you gave us, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And I'm going to suggest to you simply this: When it touched the vital interests of the HVO, there was always a way to see to it that what needed to be done was done. And when it was Muslim women in the house being raped, everybody knew. Nobody did a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The rapes in the house? They're by the HVO. They're by the Kinder Vod. That's the evidence that there's been adduced in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The question as suggested, it talks about the entire HVO. So now this is pretty broad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, I think it's specific enough for the witness to answer it, with respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In that event, Mr. President, in that event I suspect the allegation that is lodged in this question also goes to this gentleman, that now he's being accused of taking this approach, because he's a member of the HVO and he's just accused him of allowing rapes while he was in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: No, I haven't. And the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If he hasn't, then I suggest he retract that comment and he rephrase the question appropriately. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The question is entirely appropriate. I said, "Let's leave you out of the picture." It can't get clearer than that with respect. "Anybody in a command position in this area could have done what you did when there was a problem at the cafe that ended up at your barracks." I specifically left this witness out of the equation, and I appreciate my friend's sensitivity on this point, but I hope he'll agree it's misplaced on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It was possible, General --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, what's happening now with respect is that an effort is being made, I'd respectfully submit, to insulate this witness from the question, which is a fair one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness has answered all the questions up until now and he will answer, but Ms. Pinter, you're on your feet. Why?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I just wished to remind the Chamber the Praljak Defence presented a document showing that those persons were prosecuted, I thank my learned friend, Ms. Dijana, who handed a document number to me, in all that haste, 3D00422. Therefore, what the Prosecution now submits has no foundation in anything we've seen in this trial so far, quite the contrary in fact. But since they've decided to embark on the topic saying that the HVO reacted when it was in their interest and allowed those Muslim ladies to suffer, I think that is an unfair representation that is being made to the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I draw the attention of everyone to the fact that all this, in the transcript, is attributed to Judge Antonetti. You simply went much too fast. I also suspect that not little of what you have said is not correctly recorded either. I would suggest that you start anew at a speed a bit reduced.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a particularly demanding task for me. I'll try to keep it as slow as I can. My objection is to the questions asked by the Prosecutor and the misrepresentation of the facts made to this witness. During the Prosecution case in front of this very Chamber, the lady witness that the Prosecutor is now referring to was examined on the 21st of September, 2006. At the time, she was shown 3D00422, which indicates that two persons were prosecuted for acts that they committed. Therefore, this runs counter to what my learned friend from the OTP has been showing the witness. My objection was about that, about misrepresenting facts. One cannot simply state, as my learned friend Mr. Karnavas said, that the HVO in its entirety only had its own interest in mind, thereby neglecting any other circumstances that may have been involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on the transcript now. Mr. Laws, do you want to reformulate your question or do you want the witness to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Could I just reply very briefly to say that the Trial Chamber also admitted the witness statement of Witness BN, and it is perfectly clear that she describes an ongoing series of events, and the fact, if fact it be, that later some people were brought to account for it was, we respectfully submit, precious little assistance to the women in those houses during that period when they were being preyed upon. That's the point that I'm making, and I submit that that point is a perfectly fair one to make. So I'm going to move on to a different topic in just a moment, and that might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Put your question again, please, the one on the HVO, because Mr. Karnavas made an objection unless you withdraw your question because...

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I certainly don't withdraw my question. My question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then put it again to the witness, and we'll wait for the answer from the General.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: My question to you, General, is this: That the HVO were perfectly capable of deploying the military police or taking any other measures that might assist them where their own interests were at stake, their attitude to crimes committed against civilians was entirely different. Do you agree with that from your experience of being on the front line and throughout Herceg-Bosna in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm against any rape, any abuse against any civilian, and I'm aware that the military police intervened whenever it was told about these situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Even after I've shown the document from Luka Markesic saying every day, every day women and girls are taken out from the collection centres and they're raped? It was going on all the time. Nobody did anything, and I'm suggesting to you that that's because it simply wasn't a priority.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't even know if there were criminal report. I don't know anything about any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And if that is an appropriate moment to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's 20 to 6.00 we'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. As far as the IC list for tomorrow, the Petkovic Defence team, you may give us your IC list in the course of the morning. Since we will start tomorrow morning at 9.00 you might not have time, so you will be able to file your list in the middle of the morning tomorrow. The Prosecutor, in addition, has 34 minutes left so we shall give him the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: General, in 1993 or in 1994, did you ever hear that the HVO were using forced labourers to do military work?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: If you turn to the document that I hope is open for you in your bundle, because I asked for some assistance over the break so that it be ready to go, P08014. We can see a letter from the Red Cross which deals with the issue of prisoners being made to do military tasks. Have you got that letter, General?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: During its recent visits to Prozor, it's been noted that in spite of repeated oral and written interventions, so it goes on. It's a letter complaining about people being used for forced labour. There's a list of names, and then the paragraph beneath the list of names: "According to information received, several groups of civilians of the Muslim minority have been brought by force to the front line where they've had to work for several days." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: One the people to whom this was copied, General, was you as you were then Colonel Skender, commander of the south-west operational zone, HVO, Tomislavgrad, Prozor. Do you remember receiving this letter?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This note certainly reached the commander of the military area in Tomislavgrad. I was never in Tomislavgrad since I was day and night on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, it was addressed to you and to three other named people. You're saying that you simply never received it.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I never read it. If this note arrived, it must have reached Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, your answer is somewhat surprising. You are on the front line. Very well. Nobody challenges that. And then the International Red Cross sends you a letter because your name is on this letter. The letter is opened in Tomislavgrad, so an officer must have read the letter. They didn't call you up to tell you, We have a problem. The International Red Cross is sending us this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, because Tomislavgrad is quite a long way away from Prozor, and there was no administrative link between Prozor and Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were on the front line, you could not communicate with your headquarters in Tomislavgrad, with the officer who was on duty? You weren't in contact with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Over the phone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Over the phone didn't he tell you that this letter had just reached them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. This was the time when I was getting prepared or perhaps I had even left for France.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, if you turn the tab it's not the only time that the ICRC wrote to you about a totally different topic. There's nothing in this next letter of any interest at the moment, but P08089 is another letter to you in the same month. Did you receive any letters from the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So they were -- they didn't know it, but they were just wasting their time trying to contact you in this way. Is that what it comes to?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I didn't have time to look after this, even if there were serious problems. I didn't have time to deal with administrative matters. I only stayed there for two months, and I could only deal with the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, did any of the other people there named, Skender or -- I'm so sorry, I mean in the previous document, Skender, Roso, or Biskic, did any of them get in touch with you and say -- sorry, I do apologise. Roso, Siljeg, and Biskic, did any of them get in touch with you and say, We've had a letter from the Red Cross complaining about forced labour. Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I can understand that you were not aware of this, but the General Ante Roso, General Ante Roso received the letter and he was the commander of the HVO. He could have called you up to tell you, Well, Skender, what is happening? He didn't phone you up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He could have, but he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And if you go back two documents, we can see P07812 [Realtime transcript read in error "P02712"] is an order from General Roso in which he is commissioning the use of forced labour. It's February 5th of 1994. It's an order. One hundred green ants had been taken away to go to work. After the work has been completed, the commander of ZP Mostar regularly returned the ants to the anthill. And if we're in any doubt about what the anthill is, over the page we have the name "Heliodrom."

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the anthill means, and the Heliodrom was the former Heliodrom next to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, the true position was this, was it not: Roso was somebody who you said you knew by reputation from the Foreign Legion. You didn't know him personally, but you knew that he and you had both served in the Foreign Legion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And he never spoke to you about the use of forced labour?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And Siljeg. I'm not going to look at the documents for him, but Siljeg, similarly, never spoke to you about forced labour?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Siljeg not either. He never mentioned anything about forced labour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just in order to get the record straight, it's got the wrong number for the last document, and I think you misspoke. The number is 7 -- P07812, whereas the one mentioned is P02712. It's -- I invite everyone, repeatedly, to be careful about this, because the wrong number misleads us in looking for the document, so we cannot entirely follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The position, General Skender, was -- I'm going to suggest to you that it was simply common knowledge. It was very well-known by everybody who had any command position that the HVO were using forced labourers. It was common knowledge. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe, but I was not aware of that. I never saw a forced labourer on the front line or elsewhere for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Let's look at one Siljeg document then. It's P04877. He's another one of the people we've seen who's been written to by the Red Cross. Do you have that document --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could have assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 04 -- I didn't see the number. 04 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: 04877. You've not had a chance to look at that, so please look at that order from your predecessor. Have you had a chance to look at that document, General?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just read it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And we're told that in number 3, that whilst performing forced labour the -- and a derogatory term is used for the Muslim workers: "... they should not be maltreated while performing the work, but reports are to be made of the number of wounded or killed prisoners for the purposes of records." This is a forced labour programme that has casualties built into it, isn't it? I think you might be waiting for a question. I was -- sorry, waiting for an answer. You've seen Siljeg, your predecessor there, saying don't mistreat them, but if they get injured or killed, do make a report about it. He was treating this forced labour programme in a way that made it clear that casualties were inevitable, wasn't he? You can tell that from the document, can't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was true to fact my predecessor who gave this order. I was not aware of this since at the time I wasn't there. And when I arrived there, when I assumed the command, I did not know that there were any prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: But I'm putting to you that it was routine and that the commanders all knew. And we'll look at another one. Let's look at P04119. It's the fourth document from the beginning of the binder, General. P04119. And if you can find paragraph 6, we can see that another colleague of yours, Ivan Primorac, is also talking about using Muslim prisoners of war to work on the front line. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see this document. I'm actually reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And it's a document dated the 12th of August of 1993. You were with him just four days earlier, on the 8th of August. If you go back two tabs in your binder, P04062. You're out with him touring and inspecting. It's the first paragraph of that document, inspecting the front line and the troops. It's the third document in from the beginning. It records on the 8th of August you and he were touring and inspecting.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I can see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And you're saying about him, too, that you never learnt that he was ordering that prisoners of war be used on the front line? You don't -- with respect, General, you don't need to read any more of the document than that. I'm asking you really the simple question that in relation to that gentleman who you toured the lines with on the 8th of August, he's writing an order four days later for the use of prisoners of war. I'm asking you whether you ever learnt from him that --

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If you read this document, this minutes refers to military problems. I never saw a prisoner there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that the document says that you saw a prisoner. What I'm saying is that the people you're spending your time with, the people all around you, are authorising forced labour, and you happened to be one of the people the Red Cross write to about that problem as well, and I'm suggesting to you that it was common knowledge. People in your position, those around you, knew all about it, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, we have your answers. I'm going to suggest to you, finally, this, that the use of forced labour goes back to the same problem that the HVO had that led to their policy of not enforcing discipline or law and order. Shortage of troops, the easiest way to get round that have is to force the other side's captive combatants to help you, isn't it? That's exactly what was going on here I'm going to suggest to you.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I shall repeat what I have already said. I never saw a prisoner working on the front line. As far as I know there may have been some. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Were you short of troops for any reason in particular?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there was a shortage of troops. The fighters never had enough men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Was it the position that the soldiers sometimes were very happy to defend their villages but did not want to be sent further away to fight against the Muslims in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And they did not share the enthusiasm of other people in Herceg-Bosna for this war, did they?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Who are these other people who are sharing -- who have this sentiment about war? I mean, this is rather vague, I must say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, there are some sitting in the dock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I object to that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I think it's a repugnant statement to make in a court of law. We're still on trial, and he's suggesting that the gentlemen sitting in the dock were all for war and all for killing and all for raping and what have you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I find that repugnant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: No, I'm not. No, I'm not. I've put the Prosecution's case, I hope, fairly and squarely. The general has already answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Some of the people in the HVO who were soldiers sent to fight didn't want to do it, did they?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not wish to go and fight too far away from their villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And their morale fell away when they were deployed in that way, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have a follow-up question for you. You told us that you were on the front line quite often. I believe that you talked to the soldiers that were there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you talked to the soldiers. Did they tell you why they were there, as far as you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. They just said that they had been called up and that with the brigade they went up to the front line with some elements of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But they didn't say that they were there to defend their homeland, the Croats of Herceg-Bosna, or whoever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You never discussed what had prompted them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I never discussed what motivated them. I only discussed the facts, what happened on the front line, what had they done, what had they seen and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And these soldiers, didn't they ask you, "Colonel, what are we doing here"? Nobody put that kind of question to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody ever put me that question, "What are we doing here?" No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I have no more questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, do you have any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, just a couple of questions for you and then we'll be finished. Open P8889. You have the document -- P5889 is the document number. Could you have a look at that, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could ask the usher to help you out so that we can move faster and finish today. The number is written in a felt pen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What number is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: To whom is this document addressed? Look at the top there, what it says on the stamp.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was addressed to the military police and the SIS centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Don't know -- I don't know where you see "military police," but anyway. It's "military secret."

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a document dated the 15th of October, 1993, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: If it helps, I don't object to my learned friend reading what it says, and the witness can agree it -- when he sees it it'll save time. It's obvious what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I don't want to ask any leading questions. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance because on page 85, lines 19 of the transcript, two document numbers appear, so I don't know which document the witness is looking at. Perhaps my colleague could repeat the document number.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: P5889 is the number of the document. Was this document sent to the Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: P05889. I only see that the military police is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. Does it say that it was sent to the Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see "vojna tajna" instead of "policija." That's quite possible. SIS centre. I don't see who it's addressed to here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: My question was: Was it addressed to the Main Staff? Was it sent to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now take a look at another document. P4177 is the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes. Was this document sent to the -- sent to the Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A priori I don't see that it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What about the incoming stamp? Does it show that it was received by the Main Staff or the operation zone?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's the S-I-S, the SIS, but I don't see anything regarding the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you for that. Let me ask you this: Let's start at battalion level, brigade level, zone level, Main Staff level. For a commander to start any procedure whatsoever, to take any steps whatsoever, with respect to types of conduct that are not permitted, what exactly does he need to know?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first he needs to be made aware that there is a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Fine. Let's assume that he is. What else does he need to know?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assume that he knows of a problem, then immediately he must turn it over to the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That's right, but turn over to the military police just what? Does he need to know who, where, when, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he will give information on the cases that he's learned about, the fact that there was a brawl, for example, that their house was torched, that someone was killed. If -- when the unit commander knows about this, is told about this, then he asks for the military police to come over and he explains what he has just learned.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Now, General, could you please look at 3D0113. I'll try and help you find the document. And it's towards the middle or towards the end of the binder. Was this document delivered to you, General?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. At the time I was already deputy commander of the 1st Guards Corps in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. As for this document, could you please focus on the following: My learned friend from the OTP asked you about paragraph 2, talking about the showdown in Prozor town between the Garavi unit from Bugojno and the Kinder Platoon, with two members of the Kinder Platoon being killed in the clash. During your examination-in-chief and during your cross today, you referred to this event. During this showdown between the two units, one from Bugojno and the other from Rama, was there a shoot-out? Were there any wounded? Was anyone killed? Was the situation dangerous?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was one deceased and a number of injured people. And the situation was very dangerous, because some elements of the brigade were leaving the front line to go to Prozor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I'm sorry to interrupt. I believe I should have interrupted earlier, but I needed to think about the question I wanted to put to you. You said that you were the deputy commander of the 1st Guards Corps in Zagreb, line 1 and 2 of page 88. Up until now we've understood that the HVO was short of troops, of professional troops. But I mean you are a professional soldier, and you left the HVO to go to Zagreb. So how can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's because President Tudjman decided to set up a special corps who would also take into account his own security, and it was the first is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the chief of this unit was not a military, and I guess that that is the reason why the minister of defence deputised me with this person, so that this unit could operate properly, this unit called the HGZ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, we'll be going back to the showdown between Garavi and Kinder Vod. Just before the Presiding Judge's question, you mentioned that the situation was serious and difficult. The situation being what it was, you called in General Praljak; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you describe what General Praljak did? Was there any shooting going on when he first came, and how did the entire showdown end? How did things go back to calm and quiet?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He answered and said he was going to come immediately, and he arrived quickly. I don't know how long it took him, but it was quick. The military police also arrived quickly. There was no shooting at the time, but my command was encircled by the people from the Rama Brigade, and I believe that General Praljak was accompanied by a minister. I can't remember his name. Then we started talking, negotiating, actually, with the brigade, with the people who came over to get the person who was allegedly -- who had allegedly committed murders. They wanted me to hand them over, but I knew that it meant immediate death for him, so I decided that I wouldn't give in. Then after a few hours, we managed to calm things down, but we told them that this man who was in custody would be handed over to the military police. There was even a military judge who came over. And that's how the showdown ended. And all I know is that the alleged perpetrator was convicted and sentenced, but I don't know what the sentence was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Was he taken away by the military police, or was he released at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He left. He was escorted by the military police to some military gaol, but I don't know where it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: On that occasion did General Praljak not put himself in the way of danger in order to put the situation back under control, which is something that not even the military police could do? Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Praljak negotiated with them and said that he would not turn this man -- turn over this man. There was also one of his security detail that was with him. And everything -- and this guy stayed at the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, based on what you knew during your time with the HVO, was it ever the case that there was a perpetrator, a murderer, a rapist, or proven as such, was released with the procedure pending or with the procedure against him already underway?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as murder is concerned, no, absolutely not, but we had the example of Banjaluka. Only Banjaluka was report.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Banjaluka was about you. He captured you. That's how he treated you. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So throughout all of your time, the four or six months that you spent in Herzegovina, this was the only proceeding that was still pending that you were aware of, right, or that was postponed?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR SKENDER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I repeat, I did not know his resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right. The Prosecutor put something to you during one of his questions, and I will ask you to respond to that now. While asking one of his questions he said that the HVO policy was not to bring back law and order and that there policy was to back behaviour, types of behaviour, that were not permitted.
